overview: Both are interspecies relationships where at least one species benefits, but they differ in whether the other species benefits too.
genZNote: Commensalism: one friend benefits, the other genuinely doesn't care either way. Mutualism: both friends are winning.

aspects.label: Effect on Both Species
aspects.valueA: One species benefits; the other is neither helped nor harmed.
aspects.valueB: Both species benefit from the interaction.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Barnacles attaching to a whale (barnacle benefits, whale unaffected).
aspects.valueB: Bees pollinating flowers (bee gets nectar, flower gets pollinated).

aspects.label: Degree of Dependency
aspects.valueA: Often a loose, non-essential association for the unaffected partner.
aspects.valueB: Can range from optional to obligate (essential for survival, as in lichens).

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium) are the textbook example of obligate mutualism.
overlay.memoryTrick: Commensalism: one benefits, 'comme si comme ça' for the other — indifferent. Mutualism: mutual benefit for both.
overlay.commonMisconception: Commensalism does not harm the unaffected species — if harm occurs, the relationship is actually parasitism, not commensalism.
